name: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
title: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
answer: Asking data questions in plain language covers systems that let analysts, researchers, and domain experts query structured datasets without writing SQL or code. It spans natural language interfaces to databases, conversational analytics, and question answering over tables and spreadsheets. The goal is to lower the barrier between a person's question and a reproducible answer, while keeping the underlying data and query traceable. This work sits within quantitative analysis and reproducible research because the phrasing of a question shapes what is counted, filtered, or compared.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Asking data questions in plain language covers systems that let analysts, researchers, and domain experts query structured datasets without writing SQL or code. It spans natural language interfaces to databases, conversational analytics, and question answering over tables and spreadsheets. The goal is to lower the barrier between a person's question and a reproducible answer, while keeping the underlying data and query traceable. This work sits within quantitative analysis and reproducible research because the phrasing of a question shapes what is counted, filtered, or compared.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems typically run on top of existing data warehouses, relational databases, or tabular files, with a natural language layer that translates a question into a query plan. The translation layer may use a language model, a semantic parser, or a retrieval system that matches the question to known schema elements and prior queries. Compute is usually modest at query time, but model-based translation can require a GPU service or an API call before the database executes the generated query. The result is returned as a table or chart, often with the generated query shown for review.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by mapping plain language to structured operations in stages: interpreting the question, resolving entities and column names, generating a candidate query, and validating it against the schema. Many systems use few-shot prompting or fine-tuned models to convert a question into SQL or a dataframe expression, then run the query and check for empty results or type errors. Reproducibility depends on recording the original question, the generated query, the data version, and any manual edits, so that another analyst can see exactly how an answer was produced.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on who can ask what, and whether the answer can be trusted. A plain language interface can expose sensitive fields or let a user join tables in ways that reveal more than their role permits, so access controls must be enforced at the query layer, not just in the interface. There is also a risk of silent misinterpretation: a question about revenue may map to a different column than the user intended, and the system should show the generated query or a confidence note. Provenance matters because a plain language answer is only reproducible if the question, query, and data snapshot are kept together.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward interfaces that handle ambiguity through clarification rather than guessing, and that support follow-up questions, comparisons, and what-if changes in the same conversation. Systems are likely to combine a language model's flexibility with a query engine's guarantees, so that the model proposes a query but the engine validates types, permissions, and row counts. As data catalogues and semantic layers improve, plain language questions will become more reliable for routine analysis, while complex or high-stakes work will still require a human to inspect the generated query.
